# Getting Data from NEON

> **Questions**
>
> - How does NEON organize its data?
> - How do I get an API token, and how do I keep it out of my script?
> - How do I download a NEON data product into R?
> - How can code make decisions, and how does that help me download many products at once?
> - How do I check what I got?
>
> **Objectives**
>
> - Describe how NEON organizes data into sites, data products, and releases.
> - Get a NEON API token, and store it in an object without saving it in your script.
> - Download a data product with `loadByProduct()`, and describe what it returns.
> - Choose the right arguments for each product: site, dates, package, time index, and provisional data.
> - Use `if`, `else if` and `else` to make code choose between actions.
> - Use a loop to download several products, and save the results to disk.
> - Check what you downloaded, including what is missing.

The National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) measures ecosystems at sites across the United States, using the same methods at every site, and publishes the data openly. Over the next few chapters, we'll work with data from six NEON stream sites: light and water temperature recorded by sensors every 30 minutes, counts of macroinvertebrates and fish, sediment chemistry, microbes, habitat surveys, and riparian vegetation. These data are stored in many tables of different kinds, and the tables don't always agree with each other. This chapter is about getting them.

## What we are downloading

We'll use six sites, all wadeable streams, and the year 2024.

| Code | Site | State |
|------|------|-------|
| HOPB | Lower Hop Brook | Massachusetts |
| LEWI | Lewis Run | Virginia |
| POSE | Posey Creek | Virginia |
| WALK | Walker Branch | Tennessee |
| LECO | LeConte Creek | Tennessee |
| MAYF | Mayfield Creek | Alabama |

NEON publishes its data as **data products**. Each has an ID in the form `DP1.#####.###`, and we'll download ten:

| Product ID | Name | Kind |
|------------|------|------|
| DP1.20120.001 | Macroinvertebrate collection | Observations |
| DP1.20107.001 | Fish electrofishing, gill netting, and fyke netting counts | Observations |
| DP1.20277.001 | Benthic microbe group abundances | Observations |
| DP1.20086.002 | Benthic microbe community taxonomy | Observations |
| DP1.20042.001 | PAR at water surface | Sensor |
| DP1.20001.001 | Rapid habitat assessment survey | Observations |
| DP1.20191.001 | Riparian vegetation % cover | Observations |
| DP1.20194.001 | Sediment chemical and physical properties | Observations |
| DP1.20053.001 | Temperature (PRT) in surface water | Sensor |
| DP4.00130.001 | Continuous discharge | Sensor |

Sensor products are measured continuously, and NEON publishes them as averages over short intervals. We'll ask for the 30-minute averages, except for discharge, which NEON publishes as 15-minute averages. Observation products come from field and laboratory samples, collected a few times a year. A few terms will come up again and again:

- A **release** is a yearly snapshot of the data, such as `RELEASE-2026`. Released data are stable, and each release has a DOI that you can cite.
- **Provisional** data are newer than the latest release, and can still change.
- A product has a **basic** and an **expanded** package. The expanded package adds extra tables.
- The last three digits of a product ID are its revision. `DP1.20086.002` is a revision of an older product, `DP1.20086.001`, which NEON has replaced.

> **Four products need extra care**
>
> NEON announced in January 2026 that it was discontinuing two of these products, riparian vegetation % cover (`DP1.20191.001`) and benthic microbe group abundances (`DP1.20277.001`). No new data are being added to them. Data collected before the change should still be available, but we will check that 2024 is there.
>
> The rapid habitat assessment survey (`DP1.20001.001`) became its own data product in October 2026. Because it is new, its data may still be provisional, so we will ask for provisional data for that product. It is also so new that the package may not handle it smoothly yet. If its download fails, the loop below will tell you why, and carry on with the other products.
>
> Continuous discharge (`DP4.00130.001`) needs care too. NEON releases discharge data by water year, which runs from October to September, so the latest release includes discharge only through September 2024. The data for October to December 2024 are provisional and can still change, so we ask for provisional data for this product. NEON also publishes discharge as 15-minute averages, not 30-minute averages, so we ask for the 15-minute interval and will bring it into line with the other sensor data later.

## Setting up

We haven't made a repository for this work yet, and you will make one later. For now, the downloads go in their own folder on your Desktop.

1. On your Desktop, make a new folder called `neon-data`, using your computer's file manager.
2. Tell R to work in that folder with `setwd()`, which stands for "set working directory". This is the folder that R reads and writes relative paths from. Replace `yourname` with your own user name:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Mac
setwd("/Users/yourname/Desktop/neon-data")

# Windows
setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/neon-data")
```

3. Check that it worked:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getwd()
#> [1] "/Users/yourname/Desktop/neon-data"
```

If you aren't sure what your path is, find the `neon-data` folder in your file manager. On a Mac, right-click it, hold the Option key, and choose **Copy "neon-data" as Pathname**. On Windows, hold Shift, right-click it, and choose **Copy as path**. Paste the result between the quotes. On Windows, the path will use backslashes (`\`), and R needs forward slashes (`/`), so change them. If your Desktop is synced with OneDrive, the path may contain `OneDrive`, and copying the path from the file manager takes care of that.

The path printed by `getwd()` should end in `neon-data`. Every path in this chapter is relative to this folder. If you close RStudio and come back later, run the `setwd()` line again before you run anything, or the files will land somewhere else.

Choose **File > New File > R Script** and save it as `01-download-neon.R` in the `neon-data` folder. Write the code in this chapter in that script, so that you have a record of exactly what you downloaded. Start with the packages:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("neonUtilities")
library(tidyverse)
library(neonUtilities)
packageVersion("neonUtilities")
```

You only need to install a package once. The version should be 4.0.0 or higher. NEON changed how downloads work in 2026, and older versions of the package may not work with the new rules.

## Getting an API token

Since June 2026, NEON requires an **API token** to download data. A token is a long string of letters and numbers that identifies you to NEON's servers. It's free.

Go to neonscience.org, and sign in to your NEON user account, or create one. Open your account page, find the section on API tokens, generate a token, and copy it. NEON explains tokens in its API token tutorial, which you can find in its Learning Hub. A token expires after a while, and `neonUtilities` tells you when yours has, so that you can generate a new one.

Anyone who has your token can download data as you. If you paste it into a script and push that script to GitHub, it becomes public. So we will save the token in an object, and we will create that object in the **Console**, not in the script. A script is a file that gets saved and shared, but the Console is not. In the Console, run the following, with your own token in place of the example:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
token <- "paste-your-token-here"
```

The token is now stored in an object called `token`, and the code in our script will use that object, never the token itself. Check that it is there, without printing the token:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
nchar(token)
```

`nchar()` counts the characters in the text. A real token is long, so you should see a large number. Never print your token in a document you hand in. If it ever ends up on GitHub, generate a new one.

There is a cost to this. The `token` object lives in your R session, so when you close RStudio it disappears. If RStudio asks whether to save your workspace image when you quit, say **Don't Save**, and the token is not written to your computer. Each time you start a new session, run the `token <-` line in the Console again.

## Downloading one product

The function that does the work is `loadByProduct()`. We'll try it on one product at one site, to see what comes back before we ask for everything. The product is **Macroinvertebrate collection** (`DP1.20120.001`), which is the sampling of aquatic invertebrates from the stream bed. The site is HOPB (Hop Brook), and we ask for 2024 only:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
inv_test <- loadByProduct(
  dpID = "DP1.20120.001",
  site = "HOPB",
  startdate = "2024-01",
  enddate = "2024-12",
  token = token
)
```

Before it downloads anything, R works out how large the download will be, and asks: `Continuing will download files totaling approximately ... Do you want to proceed y/n:`. Type `y` and press Enter. NEON's data come in monthly packages, so any month between `startdate` and `enddate` is included in full.

The function returns a **named list**, like the ones you made in Chapter 12. Each item is a table. Let's look at what we got:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
class(inv_test)
length(inv_test)
names(inv_test)
```

Some of the names are data tables, such as `inv_fieldData` and `inv_persample`. They share a prefix that belongs to the product, here `inv_`. The rest are documentation: a table of allowed values for coded columns, `categoricalCodes_20120`, a table that defines every variable, `variables_20120`, a validation table, and a citation table. NEON asks you to cite the data you use, and the citation table is where to find how.

Look at the first rows of one data table:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
head(inv_test$inv_fieldData)
```

The column `siteID` holds the site, and `collectDate` holds the date of collection. When a column name isn't clear, the variables table defines it. It has one row for every column of every data table. Let's save it as its own object, and see what columns it has:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
variables_tbl <- inv_test$variables_20120
names(variables_tbl)
```

The column `table` says which data table a row describes, and `fieldName` says which column of that table. Now we can look up what `collectDate` means in `inv_fieldData`, by filtering the variables table:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
variables_tbl %>%
  filter(table == "inv_fieldData", fieldName == "collectDate") %>%
  select(fieldName, description, dataType, units)
```

Any other column name from `names(inv_test$inv_fieldData)` works in place of `collectDate`. If `names(variables_tbl)` shows that `description` or `units` is spelled differently, change the `select()` to match.

## Choosing the arguments

Each product needs its own settings. These are the arguments of `loadByProduct()` that matter for us:

| Argument | What it does | Our choice |
|----------|--------------|------------|
| `dpID` | The product ID | One product at a time |
| `site` | A vector of four-letter site codes | The six sites |
| `startdate`, `enddate` | The first and last month, as `"YYYY-MM"` | `"2024-01"` and `"2024-12"` |
| `package` | `"basic"` or `"expanded"` | Basic, except for the microbe taxonomy product, which needs expanded to include its per-sample taxonomy tables (`mct_benthicPerSampleTaxonomy_16S` and `mct_benthicPerSampleTaxonomy_ITS`) |
| `timeIndex` | For sensor products only, the averaging interval in minutes. `getTimeIndex()` lists the intervals a product offers | `"30"` for PAR and water temperature, and `"15"` for discharge |
| `include.provisional` | Whether to include provisional data | `FALSE`, except for the habitat and discharge products |
| `release` | Which release to download | The default, `"current"` |
| `check.size` | Whether R asks before downloading | `TRUE` at first, then `FALSE` in a script |
| `token` | Your API token | The `token` object |

The `timeIndex` argument only makes sense for sensor data. The function `getTimeIndex()` tells you which averaging intervals a product offers. Let's run it for the two sensor products:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getTimeIndex("DP1.20042.001", token = token)
getTimeIndex("DP1.20053.001", token = token)
```

Both list 30 among their intervals, in minutes, so `timeIndex = "30"` works for them. Now run it for the fish product, which is not a sensor product:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getTimeIndex("DP1.20107.001", token = token)
```

It stops with the message `DP1.20107.001 is not a streaming sensor (IS) data product; averaging interval is not relevant.` Fish counts come from field sampling, so there are no averages to choose from.

If you pass `timeIndex = "30"` to `loadByProduct()` for an observation product, it doesn't stop with an error. It prints a message for each site and month, saying that no files with that time index were found, and returns nothing. So only the two sensor products get `timeIndex = "30"`, and the rest get `"all"`.

## Making decisions with if

So far, every line of code you've run has done the same thing every time. An `if` statement lets code choose. It has a **condition** in parentheses, and some code in curly braces that runs only when the condition is `TRUE`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
x <- 5

if (x > 3) {
  print("x is bigger than 3")
}
#> [1] "x is bigger than 3"
```

The condition, `x > 3`, is an expression that comes out as `TRUE` or `FALSE`. You can run it by itself to see which. If it is `FALSE`, R skips the braces, and nothing happens. To do something else in that case, add `else`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
x <- 1

if (x > 3) {
  print("x is bigger than 3")
} else {
  print("x is 3 or smaller")
}
#> [1] "x is 3 or smaller"
```

To choose among more than two actions, add `else if`, with its own condition. R checks the conditions from the top, and runs the first block whose condition is `TRUE`. `else` goes last, and catches everything else:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
x <- 0

if (x > 3) {
  print("x is bigger than 3")
} else if (x > 0) {
  print("x is positive, but small")
} else {
  print("x is zero or negative")
}
#> [1] "x is zero or negative"
```

Two rules to remember. The condition must be a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`, so a vector of several values gives an error. And the `else` must start on the same line as the closing brace, `} else {`.

Many functions are useful in conditions because they answer a yes-or-no question. We'll use several of them in this chapter:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
file.exists("raw/fish.rds")   # is there a file with this name?
#> [1] FALSE

is.null(NULL)                 # is this object NULL, which means "nothing"?
#> [1] TRUE

is.null(5)
#> [1] FALSE

"fish" %in% c("fish", "par")  # is the item in the vector?
#> [1] TRUE
```

You can combine conditions with `&&`, which means "and", and `||`, which means "or". `!` flips a condition, so `!file.exists("raw/fish.rds")` is `TRUE` when the file is **not** there.

One more tool. Normally, an error stops your code, and a loop stops with it. The function `try()` runs some code, and if it fails, it hands back the error instead of stopping:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
result <- try(log("a"), silent = TRUE)
class(result)
#> [1] "try-error"

inherits(result, "try-error")
#> [1] TRUE
```

`log("a")` fails, because you can't take the log of text, but `try()` catches the error and saves it in `result`. `inherits(result, "try-error")` asks whether that happened, so we can use it as a condition. We'll use it to download many products without one failure ending everything.

## Downloading all of the products

Ten products with different settings are a good job for a loop, and the settings are a good job for a table. We'll write the plan as a data frame, with one row for each product:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sites <- c("HOPB", "LEWI", "POSE", "WALK", "LECO", "MAYF")

plan <- tribble(
  ~name,                 ~dpID,           ~package,   ~timeIndex, ~provisional,
  "macroinvertebrates",  "DP1.20120.001", "basic",    "all",      FALSE,
  "fish",                "DP1.20107.001", "basic",    "all",      FALSE,
  "microbe_abundance",   "DP1.20277.001", "basic",    "all",      FALSE,
  "microbe_taxonomy",    "DP1.20086.002", "expanded", "all",      FALSE,
  "par",                 "DP1.20042.001", "basic",    "30",       FALSE,
  "habitat",             "DP1.20001.001", "basic",    "all",      TRUE,
  "riparian_cover",      "DP1.20191.001", "basic",    "all",      FALSE,
  "sediment",            "DP1.20194.001", "basic",    "all",      FALSE,
  "water_temperature",   "DP1.20053.001", "basic",    "30",       FALSE,
  "discharge",           "DP4.00130.001", "basic",    "15",       TRUE
)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plan
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    name               dpID          package  timeIndex provisional
#>    <chr>              <chr>         <chr>    <chr>     <lgl>      
#>  1 macroinvertebrates DP1.20120.001 basic    all       FALSE      
#>  2 fish               DP1.20107.001 basic    all       FALSE      
#>  3 microbe_abundance  DP1.20277.001 basic    all       FALSE      
#>  4 microbe_taxonomy   DP1.20086.002 expanded all       FALSE      
#>  5 par                DP1.20042.001 basic    30        FALSE      
#>  6 habitat            DP1.20001.001 basic    all       TRUE       
#>  7 riparian_cover     DP1.20191.001 basic    all       FALSE      
#>  8 sediment           DP1.20194.001 basic    all       FALSE      
#>  9 water_temperature  DP1.20053.001 basic    30        FALSE      
#> 10 discharge          DP4.00130.001 basic    15        TRUE
```

Before the loop, decide where the files will go. Each product is saved as its own file in a `raw` folder inside `neon-data`. The path is *relative*: R reads it from your working directory, so check that `getwd()` ends in `neon-data`, or the files will land somewhere else. We'll store the folder in `neon_dir`, and `dir.create()` makes it if it doesn't exist yet:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getwd()

neon_dir <- "raw"
neon_dir

dir.create(neon_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

Now the loop goes through the rows of `plan`. For each product, it downloads the data, keeps them in a list, and saves a copy in `neon_dir`, with the product's name as the file name, such as `raw/fish.rds`. If the download stops partway, for example when your connection drops, you can run the loop again, and it skips the products that it already has:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
neon_data <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(plan))) {
  product_name <- plan$name[i]
  file_path <- file.path(neon_dir, paste0(product_name, ".rds"))

  if (file.exists(file_path)) {
    print(paste(product_name, "was already downloaded"))
    neon_data[[product_name]] <- readRDS(file_path)
    next
  }

  print(paste("Downloading", product_name))
  downloaded <- try(
    loadByProduct(
      dpID = plan$dpID[i],
      site = sites,
      startdate = "2024-01",
      enddate = "2024-12",
      package = plan$package[i],
      timeIndex = plan$timeIndex[i],
      include.provisional = plan$provisional[i],
      check.size = FALSE,
      token = token
    ),
    silent = TRUE
  )

  if (inherits(downloaded, "try-error")) {
    print(paste("Could not download", product_name))
    cat(downloaded)
  } else if (is.null(downloaded)) {
    print(paste("No data came back for", product_name))
  } else {
    neon_data[[product_name]] <- downloaded
    saveRDS(downloaded, file_path)
  }
}
```

Let's read it from the top. Each time around, `i` is the row number, so `plan$name[i]` is that row's product name, and `file_path` is where its file will be saved. `file.path()` joins the parts of a path with the right separator for your computer.

The first `if` asks whether the file already exists. If it does, we print a message, read the saved copy back with `readRDS()`, and `next` skips the rest of this trip around the loop, on to the next product. That is why running the loop a second time doesn't download anything twice.

If the file doesn't exist, we download. `try()` wraps `loadByProduct()`, so that a failure doesn't stop the loop. Then an `if`, `else if`, `else` chain decides what to do with the result:

1. If `downloaded` is a `"try-error"`, the download failed. We print which product, and `cat(downloaded)` prints the reason.
2. Otherwise, if `downloaded` is `NULL`, nothing came back, and we say so, rather than saving an empty result.
3. Otherwise, the download worked. We keep the result in `neon_data`, and `saveRDS()` saves it to disk, so that we only need to download once.

We set `check.size = FALSE` so that the loop doesn't stop and ask about each product. The first time you download a new product, it's wise to leave the default of `TRUE`, so that you can see how large the download is. This will take a while, because the sensor products are large. The loop uses the `token` object, and the token itself is never in the script, so the script is safe to share.

Run the loop, and let it finish. When it does, you'll have one `.rds` file for each product in the `raw` folder. Check that they are there, and their sizes in bytes:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
list.files(neon_dir)
file.size(list.files(neon_dir, full.names = TRUE))
```

GitHub rejects any file larger than 100 MB, so keep an eye on these. When you make your repository later, large files like these will need to be kept out of it. We'll deal with that in the next chapter.

## A problem on Windows

If you are on a Windows computer, the loop probably printed `Could not download microbe_taxonomy`, with an error saying that a zip file "cannot be opened". Nothing is wrong with the file. R downloads each product to a temporary folder deep inside your user folder, such as `C:\Users\yourname\AppData\Local\Temp\...`, and then unpacks it. The files in this product have very long names, and Windows can't create a folder when its full path is more than about 250 characters. A Mac has no such limit, so the download works there.

The fix is to download the zip files to a folder with a short path, and then unpack them from there. `zipsByProduct()` downloads the zip files without unpacking them, and `stackByTable()` unpacks them and stacks the tables, which is what `loadByProduct()` does in one step. With `savepath = "envt"`, `stackByTable()` hands back a list of tables, as `loadByProduct()` does.

We only want to do this when it is needed, which is a good job for an `if`. The condition has two parts: the product is missing from `neon_data`, and the computer is running Windows. `.Platform$OS.type` is `"windows"` on a Windows computer. The `!` in front of the first part flips it, so it is `TRUE` when `"microbe_taxonomy"` is **not** a name in `neon_data`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (!("microbe_taxonomy" %in% names(neon_data)) && .Platform$OS.type == "windows") {
  dir.create("C:/neon_zips", showWarnings = FALSE)

  zipsByProduct(
    dpID = "DP1.20086.002",
    site = sites,
    startdate = "2024-01",
    enddate = "2024-12",
    package = "expanded",
    check.size = FALSE,
    savepath = "C:/neon_zips",
    token = token
  )

  microbe_taxonomy <- stackByTable("C:/neon_zips/filesToStack20086", savepath = "envt")

  neon_data[["microbe_taxonomy"]] <- microbe_taxonomy
  saveRDS(microbe_taxonomy, file.path(neon_dir, "microbe_taxonomy.rds"))
}
```

On a Mac, the condition is `FALSE`, and nothing happens. On Windows, the data end up in `neon_data` and in `raw/microbe_taxonomy.rds`, exactly as if the loop had worked. Check:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
names(neon_data)
```

You should see all ten products.

## Checking what you downloaded

A download that finishes without an error isn't necessarily complete. Products can be empty, sites can be missing, and IDs can be wrong. We'll make three checks.

**Check the product IDs.** The function `getProductInfo()` asks NEON about a product, and returns its details, including its name in `$productName`. If the ID doesn't exist, it returns `NULL`. A loop can go through the IDs in `plan$dpID`, and an `if` can decide what to print:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (id in plan$dpID) {
  info <- getProductInfo(id, token = token)

  if (is.null(info)) {
    print(paste(id, "was not found"))
  } else {
    print(paste(id, info$productName, sep = ": "))
  }
}
```

Compare each name with the one in the table at the top of the chapter. Checking an ID against NEON's own name for it is a quick way to catch a typo, such as a missing digit, before it costs you a long download.

**Check what came back.** Which products are missing from `neon_data`? `setdiff(a, b)` returns the items of `a` that aren't in `b`, so this lists the products that didn't come back:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
setdiff(plan$name, names(neon_data))
```

Scroll back through the loop's messages to find the reason for each, and write down any that are missing. The discontinued and brand new products are the likely suspects, and we'll deal with them in the next chapter. For the products that did come back, print the names of their tables:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (product_name in names(neon_data)) {
  print(product_name)
  print(names(neon_data[[product_name]]))
}
```

**Check which sites have data.** Most NEON data tables have a `siteID` column. We want to know which sites appear in each one. This takes a loop inside a loop: the outer loop goes through the products, and the inner loop goes through the tables of each product:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (product_name in names(neon_data)) {
  for (table_name in names(neon_data[[product_name]])) {
    one_table <- neon_data[[product_name]][[table_name]]

    if (is.data.frame(one_table) && "siteID" %in% names(one_table)) {
      sites_found <- paste(sort(unique(one_table$siteID)), collapse = " ")
      print(paste(product_name, table_name, ":", sites_found))
    }
  }
}
```

The condition in the `if` has two parts joined by `&&`. The documentation items in each list aren't all data frames, and not all of the data frames have a `siteID` column. `is.data.frame(one_table)` is `TRUE` for a data frame, and `"siteID" %in% names(one_table)` is `TRUE` when it has that column. Only a table that passes both is printed. Inside the `if`, `unique()` keeps each site once, `sort()` puts them in order, and `paste(..., collapse = " ")` joins them into one piece of text.

Compare what you find with the six sites you asked for. Gaps are common in real data, because not every site collects every product every year, and it is worth knowing about them before you analyze anything.

## If something goes wrong

- **`API token was not provided, was invalid, or has expired.`** R can't find a working token. Check that `nchar(token)` prints a large number, which means the object exists, run the `token <-` line again if you restarted R, and generate a new token if yours has expired.
- **`Error: object 'token' not found`** You haven't created the `token` object in this session. Run the `token <-` line in the Console.
- **`No internet connection detected. Cannot access NEON API.`** Check your connection, and run the loop again. Products that you have already saved are skipped.
- **`Download halted.`** You answered anything other than `y` when R asked whether to proceed.
- **`There are no data at the selected site(s).` or `There are no data at the selected date(s).`** NEON has no data for that product at your sites or in your date range. The loop reports it and moves on. A product that was discontinued, or is brand new, can do this.
- **`... is not a properly formatted data product ID.`** The ID has a typo. It should look like `DP1.20120.001`.
- **`zip file ... cannot be opened` on Windows.** The path to R's temporary folder is too long. See "A problem on Windows" above.
- **The download is very slow.** The sensor products are large. Leave the loop running, and don't interrupt it. If it stops, run it again.

## Key points

- NEON organizes data into sites and data products, and each product has an ID. Check IDs, because a typo is easy to make.
- Since June 2026, downloads need a free API token. Save it in an object created in the Console, so that it never appears in your script or on GitHub.
- `loadByProduct()` returns a named list of tables, plus documentation tables that define the variables and give the citation.
- `if`, `else if` and `else` make code choose between actions, based on a condition that is `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
- `try()` lets a loop carry on after a failure, and `inherits(x, "try-error")` tells you whether one happened.
- Sensor products can be downloaded as 30-minute averages with `timeIndex = "30"`. Observation products can't. Discharge is published at 15 minutes, and by water year, so late 2024 is provisional.
- A table of settings and a loop make a repeatable download. Save the results with `saveRDS()` so that you only download once.
- After a download, check what came back, what is missing, and which sites are present.
